Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- U.S. health officials said Wednesday they have found a contaminant in a blood-thinning drug produced by Baxter Healthcare Corp. that has been linked to more than a dozen deaths in the United States. The drug can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries, and lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration launched an investigation and then a recall of some forms of the product. The scrutiny began after a spike in reports of health problems associated with heparin, a drug made by Baxter from pig intestines at plants in China and Wisconsin. Though the cause of the problems has not been determined, FDA investigators found "a heparin-like compound -- that is not heparin -- present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients" in both facilities, said Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. The contaminant, which made up 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample tested, "reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin," which explains why it was not picked up, she told reporters in a conference call. No causal link between the contaminant and the adverse events has been established yet, Woodcock said. She added that it was not clear whether the contaminant was added accidentally, as part of the processing or deliberately. It also was not clear whether the contaminant was introduced in the company's plant in Wisconsin or the one in China, Woodcock said. Though she said the exact structure of the contaminant has not been identified, "it is similar to heparin glycans." Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex class of carbohydrate. She added it was unclear whether other heparin products used outside the United States might also contain the product. Later this week, the agency will release recommendations on how manufacturers and regulators can screen for the contaminant, she said. Last year, pet food made in China was found to be tainted with an ingredient that replaced more expensive protein and that initial tests did not identify as a contaminant. Asked if the heparin contamination could be a similar case, Woodcock said, "It's possible." Doctors have used the blood-thinner for 60 years with "no history of any problems whatsoever," said the FDA commissioner, Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach. Its intravenous use can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries and lungs. Von Eschenbach said it would be "disingenuous" to expect the agency would be able to inspect "every institution in every case." Over the last fiscal year, the agency reported having inspected more than 1,000 foreign plants, a record. Since the agency issued its report that 19 deaths had been linked to the drug since January 1, 2007, it has received word of another 27 deaths, "but many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event," Woodcock said. In all, the FDA has received 785 heparin-linked reports of adverse events -- including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating and plummeting blood pressure that can lead to life-threatening shock. "They're continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this," she said. In a written statement, Baxter said its tests have suggested "that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter." Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which supplies the company with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, issued a statement saying it is working with the FDA, Baxter and outside experts to identify the cause of the adverse events. "Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause," it said. "It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events." It said that its voluntary recall of suspect product was being made as a precaution.  E-mail to a friend .

This heightened scrutiny followed an unexpected surge in reports of severe adverse health events associated with heparin, which Baxter manufactures using porcine intestinal tissue at processing plants in Wisconsin and China. 

While the exact cause of these health issues has yet to be finalized, FDA investigators detected "a heparin-like compound—that is not heparin—present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients" at both facilities, according to Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. Speaking during a media teleconference, Dr. Woodcock explained that the contaminant comprised 5 to 20 percent of the tested samples and "reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests," which explains why standard quality controls failed to detect it. She added that a definitive causal link between the contaminant and the reported adverse events has not yet been established.

Dr. Woodcock stated it remains unclear whether the contaminant was introduced accidentally during processing or added deliberately, nor is it known whether it entered the supply chain at the Wisconsin facility or the plant in China. Although the precise molecular structure has not been fully identified, she noted that "it is similar to heparin glycans"—glycans being complex carbohydrates known as polysaccharides. It is also uncertain whether heparin products distributed outside the United States may contain the same substance. Later this week, the agency plans to issue screening recommendations to assist manufacturers and regulators in detecting the contaminant. 

When asked if this incident might parallel a previous case involving pet food imported from China—where an undetected additive was used to artificially boost protein readings—Dr. Woodcock conceded, "It's possible."

FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach noted that clinicians have safely administered this intravenous blood-thinner for 60 years with "no history of any problems whatsoever." Addressing regulatory oversight, Dr. von Eschenbach remarked that it would be "disingenuous" to expect the FDA to inspect "every institution in every case," though he highlighted that the agency conducted a record high of over 1,000 foreign plant inspections during the previous fiscal year.

Following an initial report linking 19 deaths to the drug since January 1, 2007, the agency has received notification of an additional 27 fatalities; however, Dr. Woodcock clarified that "many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event." In total, the FDA has logged 785 adverse event reports related to heparin, with symptoms including respiratory distress, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating, and severe blood pressure drops capable of inducing life-threatening shock. "They're continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this," Dr. Woodcock said.

In a written statement, Baxter indicated that internal testing suggests "the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter." 

Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC (SPL), the supplier of the active pharmaceutical ingredients to Baxter, issued a statement confirming it is collaborating with the FDA, Baxter, and external experts to determine the source of the issue. "Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause," the company stated, adding, "It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events." SPL emphasized that its voluntary recall of the suspect product was undertaken strictly as a precautionary measure.

**Unmasking the Contaminant: The 2008 Heparin Crisis and the Evolution of Global Drug Safety**

In late 2007 and early 2008, hospitals across the United States began reporting an alarming and unprecedented trend. Patients undergoing routine medical procedures—ranging from kidney dialysis to open-heart surgery—were suddenly experiencing severe allergic reactions. Symptoms included rapid, dangerous drops in blood pressure, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, and anaphylactic shock. Tragically, for dozens of patients, these adverse reactions proved fatal. The common thread uniting these disparate cases was quickly identified: every affected patient had been administered heparin, a vital blood-thinning medication manufactured by Baxter Healthcare Corp.

As public health alarm grew, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) launched a comprehensive, high-priority investigation to isolate the cause of the contamination. Because heparin is derived from raw biological material—specifically, the mucosal lining of pig intestines—tracing its origin required untangling a complex, international supply chain. FDA investigators focused their efforts on analyzing raw Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) and finished products collected from key nodes in Baxter’s supply chain, including processing facilities in Wisconsin and raw-material supplier plants in China.

Initial testing posed a significant puzzle: the tainted drug batches had successfully passed all standard quality control assays required by the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) at the time. However, advanced chemical analysis using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and capillary electrophoresis finally unmasked the culprit. Investigators discovered a counterfeit substance integrated directly into the crude heparin batches. 

The contaminant was identified as oversulfated chondroitin sulfate (OSCS), a chemically modified animal byproduct that closely mimicked the molecular structure, charge, and physical properties of real heparin. Because OSCS so effectively copied heparin's natural characteristics, it completely evaded traditional quality-assurance tests, allowing it to slip past routine factory screenings undetected. Chemical analyses revealed that this synthetic imposter comprised between 5 and 20 percent of the active ingredient in the affected lots. Once injected into the bloodstream, OSCS activated inflammatory pathways in the human body, triggering the sudden, severe anaphylactoid reactions that proved fatal to vulnerable patients.

The discovery that the contamination was likely a case of economically motivated adulteration—a deliberate attempt to stretch raw materials using a cheaper, dangerous substitute—sent shockwaves through the pharmaceutical industry and regulatory bodies worldwide. In response, Baxter initiated a massive recall of all its multi-dose heparin vials, preventing further casualties.

The crisis marked a pivotal turning point in global pharmaceutical oversight. Recognizing the vulnerabilities of an increasingly international supply chain, the FDA moved rapidly to establish new, far more stringent screening protocols. The agency mandated the use of sophisticated analytical testing methods capable of detecting OSCS and other subtle adulterants in raw materials before they could be processed into finished medications. Furthermore, the event prompted structural changes within the FDA, leading to increased foreign manufacturing inspections, stricter standard monographs, and heightened vigilance regarding the global sourcing of active drug ingredients. Today, the 2008 heparin crisis remains a landmark case study in the critical necessity of rigorous, evolving drug safety standards.

**Baxter Healthcare Recalls Blood Thinner Following Discovery of Contaminated Chinese Ingredients**

**WASHINGTON** — Healthcare giant Baxter International Inc. has expanded a nationwide recall of its widely used injectable blood-thinner heparin following evidence that active ingredients sourced from Chinese processing plants were contaminated with a dangerous foreign substance. 

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and health officials nationwide have linked the adulterated batches to hundreds of severe adverse reactions, including severe allergic shocks, a rapid drop in blood pressure, and over 80 reported deaths across the United States.

Heparin, a critical anticoagulant derived from pig intestines, is standardly administered in hospitals during heart surgeries, kidney dialysis, and to prevent blood clots in critically ill patients. Baxter supplies nearly half of the U.S. market for the multi-dose vials of the drug.

According to federal regulators, chemical analysis revealed that raw batches of the active pharmaceutical ingredient were contaminated with oversulfated chondroitin sulfate (OSCS)—a chemically modified compound derived from animal cartilage. Because OSCS mimics the molecular behavior of heparin, it bypassed routine quality-control tests while drastically lowering production costs for raw material suppliers.

"This appears to be a case of deliberate adulteration rather than an accidental chemical spill," said federal officials during a press briefing, noting that the contaminant was blended into the supply chain prior to reaching Baxter’s manufacturing facilities.

The supply chain for the raw materials has been traced back to unregulated consolidators and "workshop" processors in China, which supplied raw crude heparin to Changzhou SPL, a Chinese facility majority-owned by Wisconsin-based Scientific Protein Laboratories. Changzhou SPL subsequently supplied the active ingredient to Baxter. 

The crisis has exposed significant vulnerabilities in the globalized pharmaceutical supply chain. FDA inspectors admitted that the Changzhou SPL facility had never been inspected by U.S. regulators prior to the outbreak due to a clerical mix-up involving similar facility names in federal databases. 

"We are deeply saddened by the patient outcomes associated with these recalled products," Baxter said in a statement. "We are working around the clock with the FDA and international authorities to isolate the source of contamination, secure alternative supplies, and ensure the safety of the medical supply chain."

In response to the recall, hospitals across the nation have been forced to scramble for alternative suppliers, such as APP Pharmaceuticals, to avoid critical shortages of the life-saving medication. The FDA has since issued revised testing guidelines, requiring all manufacturers importing heparin into the United States to use advanced testing methods—including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy—capable of detecting the OSCS contaminant.

The incident has sparked sharp criticism on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers are calling for mandatory FDA inspections of overseas drug manufacturing plants and stricter origin-labeling laws for active pharmaceutical ingredients. 

Health officials advise hospitals and healthcare facilities to immediately segregate and return any remaining inventory of Baxter’s multi-dose heparin vials while federal and international criminal investigations into the supply chain continue.

**FDA Identifies Foreign Contaminant in Recalled Heparin; Supply Chain Under Scrutiny**

**By Health News Desk**  
**WASHINGTON — March 6, 2008**

Federal health regulators announced today that scientists have identified a mysterious, chemically altered contaminant in batches of the widely used blood-thinning drug heparin manufactured by Baxter Healthcare Corp. The discovery marks a critical breakthrough in an expanding public health investigation into hundreds of severe allergic-type reactions and at least 19 patient deaths reported across the United States since late last year.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revealed that the foreign substance closely resembles heparin, making it virtually undetectable using standard screening tests previously required by the U.S. Pharmacopeia. 

"We have identified a contaminant that mimics heparin in standard test procedures," said Dr. Janet Woodcock, director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, during a press briefing Thursday morning. "This substance appears to be a chemically modified compound—specifically, a sulfated derivative of chondroitin. We are working around the clock to determine whether this was an intentional adulteration or an accidental breakdown in the complex global supply chain."

Dr. Woodcock added that the agency has not yet definitively proven that the contaminant caused the severe side effects—which include rapid drops in blood pressure, breathing difficulties, nausea, and vomiting—but noted that the compound was found in high concentrations in batches of the drug associated with patient reactions.

### A Critical Life-Saving Drug Compromised

Heparin is a vital anticoagulant used daily in hospitals nationwide to prevent blood clots during open-heart surgery, kidney dialysis, and blood transfusion procedures. 

The crisis began in January when clinicians at several hospitals reported an unprecedented spike in acute allergic reactions in patients receiving high-dose intravenous heparin. In response, Deerfield, Ill.-based Baxter Healthcare voluntarily recalled its multi-dose vials of injectable heparin in early February and subsequently suspended all production of the product.

In a statement released Thursday, Baxter expressed support for the FDA's findings and reiterated its commitment to patient safety.

"Our top priority remains the health and well-being of the patients who rely on our products," Baxter Healthcare Corp. said in a written statement. "Baxter has been working closely and transparently with the FDA, independent academic experts, and our raw material suppliers to isolate the root cause of these adverse events. We fully support the FDA’s identification of this foreign substance and are focusing all available resources on tracing how it entered the raw material stream."

### Tracking the Supply Chain to China

The discovery has turned intense international attention toward the global pharmaceutical supply chain. Heparin is traditionally derived from the mucus of pig intestines. The raw material, known as "crude heparin," is largely gathered from thousands of small artisanal workshops and processing facilities in China before being refined.

Baxter’s crude heparin was supplied by Scientific Protein Laboratories (SPL), a company based in Waunakee, Wisconsin. SPL operates a major processing joint venture in China, Changzhou SPL, located in Jiangsu province, where the crude material underwent initial purification before being shipped to the U.S.

In a statement issued Thursday, SPL defended its commitment to safety while acknowledging the ongoing investigation at its overseas and domestic facilities.

"Scientific Protein Laboratories is dedicated to the highest standards of safety and quality control," the company stated. "We are working collaboratively with the FDA and our corporate partners to identify the source of the contaminant identified today. SPL is conducting rigorous audits of every level of our supply chain—from raw material collection in China to final processing—to ensure our products meet all safety specifications."

The FDA acknowledged today that it had not inspected the Changzhou SPL facility prior to the outbreak of adverse events, citing a case of mistaken identity in its tracking database that led inspectors to confuse the plant with another facility. FDA officials confirmed that an inspection team is currently on the ground in China investigating the site and its raw material suppliers.

### New Testing Mandated to Protect Patients

To prevent further contaminated blood thinners from reaching American patients, the FDA announced today that it has developed two advanced testing methods—nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and capillary electrophoresis—capable of detecting the newly identified contaminant. 

The agency is now requiring all manufacturers selling heparin in the United States to test both crude and refined stocks using these advanced methods before releasing any product to the market.

While Baxter’s withdrawal of heparin created temporary localized shortages, health officials noted that competing manufacturers, including APP Pharmaceuticals, have stepped up production to fill the market void. However, Dr. Woodcock warned that caution remains necessary as the FDA screens the entire nation's heparin supply.

"We are taking every step necessary to protect the American public and secure the drug supply," Dr. Woodcock said. "While our immediate priority is ensuring the safety of heparin currently on hospital shelves, this situation underscores the urgent need for enhanced oversight of globalized pharmaceutical manufacturing."

**FDA Orders Mass Recall of Pig-Derived Blood Thinner Amid Toxic Contamination: Echoes of Past Pet Food Crisis Resurface**

**WASHINGTON** — Federal health authorities issued an urgent global recall on Tuesday for several batches of a critical blood-thinning medication after tests revealed the active ingredient—derived from pig intestines—was contaminated with a hazardous synthetic compound. 

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA), acting in coordination with European health regulators, ordered the immediate withdrawal of the affected injectable anticoagulants. The move comes after dozens of patients across multiple countries suffered severe allergic reactions, rapid drops in blood pressure, and several reported fatalities linked to the tainted batches.

The recalled medication relies heavily on crude heparin, an active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) extracted from the mucosal lining of pig intestines. Investigators believe the contaminant was deliberately introduced high up in the supply chain to stretch raw material supplies and boost profits—a practice known in regulatory circles as "economic adulteration."

For public health experts, the unfolding crisis carries a chilling sense of déjà vu, drawing direct parallels to the devastating tainted pet food scandal that triggered nationwide panic nearly two decades ago.

### A Deadly Strategy of "Economic Adulteration"

Preliminary laboratory analyses indicate that the pig-derived API was spiked with a cheap, chemically altered byproduct that mimics the molecular structure of genuine heparin. Because standard quality-control tests only measure basic biological activity, the counterfeit compound successfully bypassed routine screening at processing facilities.

The mechanism of deception is virtually identical to the 2007 pet food scandal originating from China, which resulted in the deaths of thousands of cats and dogs across North America. In that incident, rogue suppliers mixed melamine—a nitrogen-rich chemical used in plastics and fertilizers—into wheat gluten and rice protein concentrates. The additive tricked standard lab tests into reading artificially elevated protein levels, allowing suppliers to sell sub-standard ingredients at premium prices. 

"What we are seeing today is the pharmaceutical equivalent of the melamine crisis," said Dr. Aris Thorne, a supply chain security analyst at the Global Health Policy Institute. "In both cases, bad actors exploited a flaw in standard testing protocols by introducing a dangerous, look-alike chemical into an organic raw material. It is a calculated, profit-driven crime with lethal consequences."

### The Vulnerability of the Organic Supply Chain

The recall highlights the unique vulnerabilities inherent in bio-derived pharmaceuticals. Unlike synthetic drugs created in controlled chemical laboratories, pig-derived APIs depend on vast agricultural supply chains. 

China, home to the world’s largest pig population, supplies over 60 percent of the global crude heparin market. The raw material is typically gathered from thousands of small-scale slaughterhouses and localized rendering plants before being consolidated, processed, and shipped to international pharmaceutical manufacturers. 

Regulators acknowledge that tracing raw animal tissue through thousands of informal collection sites poses monumental challenges. 

"When your raw material starts in a slaughterhouse rather than a sterile lab, supply chain transparency becomes exponentially harder to enforce," Thorne added. "Just as melamine exposed the cracks in global agricultural trade, this recall exposes how deeply reliant Western medicine is on unverified overseas raw material hubs."

### Regulators Move to Tighten Controls

In response to the recall, the FDA has mandated that all imports of pig-derived APIs undergo advanced testing—including high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy—capable of detecting subtle molecular anomalies that traditional screens miss.

Major hospital networks have begun pulling the affected lots from operating rooms and dialysis units, scrambling to secure alternative supplies of the vital drug. Health officials warned that while immediate patient safety is the priority, the widespread recall could lead to temporary shortages of critical anticoagulants.

Legislators on Capitol Hill are already calling for congressional hearings, pressing the FDA to explain how contaminated animal products once again penetrated the global medical supply chain. 

As investigations continue into the specific facilities responsible for the tainted pig mucosa, health advocates argue that structural change is long overdue. 

"We learned with pet food that cost-cutting in distant supply chains can have fatal results at home," said Eleanor Vance, a patient advocacy representative. "To see the exact same trick played out in life-saving human medicine is unforgivable. Relying on uninspected, animal-derived imports without rigorous oversight is a gamble we can no longer afford to take."
